passage: The auto was stuck on the Lucknow ring road in a drizzle, and Pema, three weeks into her college year, pressed her face to the plastic window. First came a crowd dancing behind a white horse, dhol thundering, a man tossing coins into the air. "Wedding," Lalit said, grinning. "The groom's side, the baraat. They'll dance all the way to the venue." Pema laughed and filmed a few seconds. Twenty minutes later a second procession passed on foot, slower: men in white carrying a bamboo bier covered in marigolds, chanting in low voices. Pema started to raise her phone again, then stopped. Their faces were different. "Is this also a celebration?" she whispered. "No," Lalit said quietly. "A funeral. They're going to the ghat." Pema lowered the phone and bowed her head until they had passed. "In Gangtok our funeral processions have monks and prayer flags," she said. "I wouldn't have known this one." "That's why you asked," Lalit said.

qa.q: What were the men in the second procession carrying?
qa.a: A bamboo bier covered in marigolds.

qa.q: Why did Pema stop raising her phone at the second procession?
qa.a: Pema felt unsure and cautious, sensing from the slow pace, white clothes, low chanting and faces that this was different, so she chose respect over filming.

qa.q: What did Pema do that an outsider should do?
qa.a: Watch respectfully, lower the phone, and quietly ask what the procession meant.

qa.q: How might the mourners have felt if Pema had filmed them?
qa.a: Probably intruded upon at a moment of grief.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult outsider reading a baraat as joy and a funeral procession as loss, observing respectfully and asking rather than guessing.

passage: The climate march through Guwahati began at the college gate at ten, and by noon the heat was brutal. Lakshmi walked near the front with a cardboard sign, "Save our wetlands," chanting with the others until her throat was raw. Before starting, she and Bhupen had agreed on two things: stay near the volunteers in green caps, and if they got separated, meet at the bookshop on the corner of the lane behind the stadium. Near the district office the police had set up barricades. Most marchers stopped, sang and sat down on the road as planned. But a handful at the back started shoving and shouting at the officers. The crowd tightened. Lakshmi looked round; Bhupen was gone. Her heart thumped. She stepped sideways out of the press, followed a green cap to the lane behind the stadium, and texted him. Ten minutes later he appeared at the bookshop with two bottles of water. "Did the pushing start near you?" he asked. "Yes. So I left."

qa.q: Where had they agreed to meet if they got separated?
qa.a: At the bookshop on the corner of the lane behind the stadium.

qa.q: How did Lakshmi feel when the crowd tightened and Bhupen was gone?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt anxious and frightened, heart thumping, yet stayed calm enough to follow their plan.

qa.q: Which safety steps helped Lakshmi during the march?
qa.a: Agreeing a meeting point in advance, staying near the volunteers, and stepping out of the crowd as soon as the pushing started.

qa.q: How might the officers at the barricade have seen the march?
qa.a: Mostly as a peaceful sit-in with singing, with tension coming only from the few who shoved.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult voicing a cause through a peaceful march with chants and signs, while staying aware of safety and exit routes.

subtype: Grateful, welcoming and joyful in new communities [Interpreting]
passage: On Rajni's third night at the working women's hostel in Bengaluru, someone knocked with a steel plate of holige, still warm. "My amma sent a whole box," said Sharmila from the next room. "You're from Jaipur, no? Try." Rajni hesitated. In her old flat, neighbours never knocked unless something was wrong. Was this a welcome, or just extra sweets? She thanked Sharmila twice, perhaps too formally. Sharmila waved it away. "Arre, no thank-you between neighbours." The next evening Rajni found a note under her door: "Rangoli on the terrace, Sunday. Come." On Sunday she climbed up, unsure, and five women made space on the mat without a word, handing her a tin of coloured powder. Nobody thanked anyone for anything; they simply passed things along. On Monday Rajni bought a box of ghevar near the bus stand and left it on Sharmila's shelf, with no note. That night Sharmila texted one line: "Ghevar! Now you're one of us."

qa.q: What sweet did Sharmila bring?
qa.a: Holige, still warm.

qa.q: Why did Rajni hesitate at Sharmila's knock?
qa.a: Rajni felt unsure and a little wary, since in the old flat neighbours only knocked when something was wrong.

qa.q: How did Rajni learn to return the welcome?
qa.a: By joining the terrace rangoli and then leaving ghevar on Sharmila's shelf, showing thanks through sharing, the way the hostel did.

qa.q: How did Sharmila see Rajni's repeated thanks?
qa.a: As unneeded formality between neighbours, since for her gratitude is shown by sharing, not saying 🙂

grounding: It illustrates a young adult in a new city reading shared sweets and invitations as welcome, and learning how local custom shapes the way thanks is expressed.

subtype: Loving and admiring in adult relationships [Expressing]
passage:
Tuesday
Tonight I asked Amandeep something I should have asked months ago: "What makes you feel most cared for?" I've been sending good-morning messages every day, songs, little hearts, because that's how I feel loved. Amandeep laughed and said, "The messages are sweet. But honestly? When you came and sat with me at the hospital while Papa had his scans, and didn't try to fix anything, that's when I felt it most." I almost didn't go that day; I thought I'd be in the way. Amandeep's way of loving me, I realised, is fixing my cycle chain without being asked and remembering my exam dates. Mine is words. Neither is wrong. We just speak different dialects. We made a small plan: fewer songs, more Sunday walks, and I'll ask before assuming a message is enough. I also thought about Prof. Kulkarni today, and how much I admire the way she listens. Maybe I'll tell her that too.
Deepak

qa.q: Where did Deepak sit with Amandeep?
qa.a: At the hospital while Papa had his scans.

qa.q: How did Deepak feel on learning what made Amandeep feel cared for?
qa.a: Deepak felt surprised and a little humbled, and glad about going to the hospital after almost staying away.

qa.q: What plan did they make?
qa.a: Fewer songs, more Sunday walks, and Deepak asking rather than assuming a message is enough.

qa.q: What makes Amandeep feel most cared for?
qa.a: Quiet presence and time, like being sat with at the hospital without anyone trying to fix things.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult showing love through messages, time and help, and asking a partner what feels caring rather than assuming.

subtype: Grieving and sorrowful away from home [Regulating]
passage:
Dear Suraj,
Thank you for calling every night this week, even when I barely said anything. I know Maa told you I'm "handling it well." That's the face I've been wearing in the hostel. The truth is, missing Nani's last rites in Dibrugarh has felt like standing outside a closed door. Everyone at home was together, and I was here writing a lab report.
Two things helped. On Saturday my roommate Farzana and I cooked Nani's masor tenga in the hostel kitchen, badly, and I lit a small lamp beside her photo on my desk. Farzana didn't ask questions; she just ate two helpings. And on Monday I went to the student counsellor, who said grief far from home often gets pushed down because there's no one around to grieve with. That made sense.
I'm not okay yet. But I'm less alone than I was last week.
Your didi,
Rekha

qa.q: What dish did Rekha and Farzana cook?
qa.a: Nani's masor tenga.

qa.q: What was Rekha feeling behind the brave face?
qa.a: Rekha felt shut out and lonely, like standing outside a closed door, grieving far away while the family was together.

qa.q: What helped Rekha begin to heal?
qa.a: Marking the loss with Nani's dish and a lamp, a roommate's quiet company, Suraj's calls, and a visit to the student counsellor.

qa.q: How might Suraj feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Probably relieved that Rekha is being honest and getting support, after hearing only that Rekha was "handling it well".

grounding: It illustrates a young adult grieving far from family behind a brave face, and easing it through ritual, friends, family calls and a counsellor.

subtype: Angry and irritated in shared living and study [Regulating]
passage: By the second week in the engineering college hostel, Tarun had counted it: Chetan's speaker came on at eleven-thirty every night, bass thumping through the bunk. On Monday Tarun pulled his pillow over his head. On Tuesday he slammed his cupboard door, hoping that would say it for him. It didn't. On Wednesday, lying awake at one, he caught himself drafting a furious speech in his head, words he knew he'd regret. So he got up, walked to the common room, drank a glass of water, and wrote down what he actually needed. On Thursday afternoon, when both of them were relaxed, he said, "Can I bring up something small before it becomes big? The music after eleven is keeping me up, and I've got eight o'clock labs." Chetan blinked. "Seriously? Why didn't you say? I thought you liked it." They settled on headphones after eleven, and Tarun's cupboard door stayed quiet.

qa.q: What time did Chetan's speaker come on each night?
qa.a: At eleven-thirty.

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling by Wednesday night?
qa.a: Tarun's irritation had built into real anger, enough to draft a furious speech he knew he'd regret.

qa.q: What stopped the irritation turning into a fight?
qa.a: Taking a break to walk and write down the need, then raising it early and calmly at a relaxed moment with a specific request.

qa.q: How had Chetan read Tarun's silence and the slammed door?
qa.a: He hadn't understood them at all; he thought Tarun liked the music.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult noticing irritation building with a roommate, taking a break, and naming the issue early in calm words before it becomes conflict.

subtype: Fearful and alarmed in unsafe situations [Interpreting]
passage: I run the chemist's shop by the bus stop, and I'm open till eleven. Last Thursday, around ten, a young woman came in fast and stood close to the counter, not looking at the shelves. Seema, I learned later. She kept glancing at the glass door. Outside, a man in a grey jacket had stopped under the streetlight, pretending to read his phone. He'd walked past twice already. Seema said quietly, "I think he's been following me from the station. Can I wait here?" I can't say he was following her; he might have been waiting for someone. But she looked frightened, and her hands were shaking on her bag strap. I said, "Stay as long as you like," and pulled a stool round. She called her friend Kiran, who said they'd come on the scooter in ten minutes. I also rang the beat constable, whose number I keep by the till. By the time the constable walked up, the man in grey had gone. Kiran arrived, and they left together.

qa.q: Until what time is the chemist's shop open?
qa.a: Till eleven.

qa.q: What was Seema feeling when she came into the shop?
qa.a: Seema felt frightened and alarmed, sensing she was being followed, with shaking hands and eyes on the door.

qa.q: Which of Seema's steps were sound?
qa.a: Moving into a lit public shop, asking to wait there, and calling a friend to come, while the shopkeeper rang the beat constable.

qa.q: How did the shopkeeper read the situation?
qa.a: The shopkeeper was unsure whether the man was really following her, but took her fear seriously enough to let her wait and call the constable.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult treating a gut sense of being followed as a cue, moving to a public place and asking for help, while the danger itself stays uncertain.

passage:
Parul found Lavanya on the hostel terrace, knees pulled up, results open on her phone.
"Hey. Can I sit?"
Lavanya shrugged. Parul sat down, not too close.
"I failed maths. Again. Everyone else is posting their marks."
"That sounds really heavy."
"Don't tell me about the supplementary exam. I know."
"I wasn't going to. I'm just here."
For a while neither spoke. Below, someone was singing badly in the mess.
"I feel so stupid," Lavanya said at last. "Papa's going to go quiet in that way he does."
"You're not stupid. You're disappointed, and dreading that silence. Both make sense."
Parul hesitated, then asked gently, "Can I check one thing? Are you feeling safe? Any thoughts of hurting yourself?"
"No. Nothing like that. Just tired and ashamed."
"Thank you for telling me. If that ever changes, even a little, we go to the counsellor together, straight away."
Lavanya leaned her head on Parul's shoulder. "Can we just sit a bit longer?"
"As long as you like."

qa.q: Which subject did Lavanya fail?
qa.a: Maths.

qa.q: Why did Parul sit down not too close and say "I'm just here"?
qa.a: Parul felt concerned and wanted to be caring without crowding Lavanya or rushing to fix things.

qa.q: How did Parul's support help more than quick advice would have?
qa.a: Parul sat, listened and named the feelings without fixing, checked gently on safety, and had a clear plan to go to the counsellor together if things changed.

qa.q: What was it like for Lavanya when Parul didn't mention the supplementary exam?
qa.a: It likely felt like relief: Lavanya didn't have to defend herself and could admit feeling stupid and ashamed.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult sitting and listening with a distressed friend without quick fixes or judgement, and checking on safety so professional help can follow if needed.

subtype: Puzzled and confused in video calls [Mismatch]
passage: At the community centre's online tutoring training, Avni was running her first video session for new volunteers. Halfway through her slide on lesson plans, she noticed Suraj's square: face frozen, eyes turned to the side, microphone muted. Was he lost? Bored? Had his connection dropped? In a room she'd have seen him lean forward or frown. Here she had one still picture. Avni paused. "Quick check before I go on. Suraj, and everyone, can you type in the chat: clear, a bit lost, or my video froze?" Three people typed "clear." Then Suraj's square moved, and he unmuted, a little sheepish. "Sorry, my screen froze for a second, and then I was looking at notes on my other monitor. Honestly, I'm a bit lost on the lesson-plan part." "Thanks for saying so," Avni said. "Let me show you an example." Afterwards she added a quick check-in every ten minutes to her slides.

qa.q: Which three options did Avni ask people to type?
qa.a: Clear, a bit lost, or my video froze.

qa.q: How was Suraj feeling when he unmuted?
qa.a: Suraj felt a little sheepish and confused, admitting he was lost on the lesson-plan part.

qa.q: What made Avni's check-in useful?
qa.a: She asked in words with easy options instead of guessing from a frozen face, and then built regular check-ins into her slides.

qa.q: How did Suraj's square look to Avni before she asked?
qa.a: Hard to read: frozen, looking away and muted, so he might have been lost, bored or simply lagging.

grounding: It illustrates how a frozen, muted face on a video call can mean thinking, lag or confusion, and how checking in with words replaces the missing cues.

passage: I'm Dolma, and in my first year of the psychology course I became the class sceptic. A lecturer quoted a study claiming that students who study with music remember less; I asked how many students, which music, and who paid for it. Good questions, the lecturer said, and we looked up the paper together: forty students, one kind of music, a single test. Useful to know. I got a taste for it. By the second term I was rolling my eyes at everything. When Zeenat shared a large review on sleep and memory for our group project, I said, "Studies can prove anything," and wouldn't read it. Zeenat went quiet, then said, "You're not being sceptical. You're just refusing." That stung, mostly because she was right. I read the review that night. It covered dozens of studies, with methods explained clearly. Now I try to ask the same questions of everything, including my own doubts, and then actually listen to the answers.

qa.q: How many students were in the music study?
qa.a: Forty.

qa.q: How did Dolma feel when Zeenat said "You're just refusing"?
qa.a: Dolma felt stung and a little ashamed, mostly because Zeenat was right.

qa.q: How does Dolma now keep scepticism fair?
qa.a: By asking the same questions of every claim, including Dolma's own doubts, and actually listening to the answers.

qa.q: How might Zeenat have felt when Dolma dismissed the review unread?
qa.a: Frustrated and brushed aside, having brought solid evidence to the group project.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult questioning sources and methods fairly, then sliding into dismissive cynicism and returning to curious, fair scepticism.
